name: Adhesive foot detox pads

card.summary: Sticky pads worn on the soles overnight and marketed as drawing out toxins, used by people hoping for a clearer, fresher-looking complexion and general wellness.
card.note: Darkened pads are attributed by researchers and journalists to the pad ingredients reacting with moisture rather than to toxins.

quick.overview:
Adhesive foot detox pads are patches stuck to the soles of the feet, usually overnight, and sold on the claim that they pull toxins out of the body through the skin. Proponents in wellness circles link detoxing to clearer skin, better energy and a healthier look.

The pad typically turns dark by morning, which sellers present as visible proof of toxins leaving. Commentators who have examined related foot-detox products report that the colour change comes from the product itself reacting with moisture. No published trials of the pads on skin appearance were found.
quick.how: Users place a pad on each sole before bed, leave it on overnight, and remove it in the morning, often as part of a wider detox or wellness routine.
quick.risks: Adhesive on the soles can irritate skin in some users. The main reported downside is the cost of a product whose stated mechanism has not been demonstrated by testing.

lead: Adhesive foot detox pads are single-use patches applied to the soles of the feet, typically overnight, and marketed as removing toxins from the body. Within appearance-focused communities the idea is attached to a chain of benefits: fewer toxins, then clearer skin, better sleep and energy, and a fresher look.

The pads belong to the wider family of foot detox products, which also includes ionic foot baths. Wikipedia describes foot baths as devices in which electrodes in salty water rust and turn the water brown, a result that researchers and journalists who tested them attribute to the electrodes rather than the body.[1] Writers who have examined these products, such as Ben Goldacre and Joe Schwarcz, reported that the residue was iron oxide and that no body-derived waste such as urea or creatinine was found.[1]
No published clinical studies of adhesive foot pads and skin appearance were found.

chain: Believed toxin removal supports clearer skin and general wellness
angle.text: Users wear the pads hoping that removing toxins will show up as healthier skin and more energy. The visible darkening of the pad is what many treat as the sign that it is working.

infobox: Draws toxins out through the skin

paras: The pads are sold as patches containing plant extracts or minerals and stuck to the foot arch overnight. Sellers describe the dark residue found in the morning as the toxins that were drawn out.

Ionic foot baths became popular with consumers in the early 2000s and spread to spas, partly because of the dramatic brown water they produce.[1] Proponents say they rebalance the body and help with headaches, sleep and organ function, while some spas use colour charts linking water shade to organs.[1]

In a 2011 television segment an engineer concluded that the residue was rust from the metal electrodes, and Goldacre reproduced the effect with a car battery, nails and water.[1] Water tested by his team showed a rise in iron but no urea or creatinine.[1]

Foot pads appear on the fringe of detox and skin-care discussion as a low-effort overnight step. Practitioners describe the pad colour change as their evidence; researchers who examined foot baths describe a chemical reaction rather than elimination of toxins.[1]

timeline.event: Ionic foot baths become popular with consumers and spas.[1]
A television segment has an engineer examine a foot bath and attribute the residue to rust.[1]

lore.intro: Foot pads are discussed within wider detox and wellness circles as an overnight add-on to skin care.

claims.claim: The pad turns dark because it pulls toxins from the body
claims.believers: Proponents point to the dark colour of the used pad as visible evidence of toxin removal.
claims.experts: Testers of related foot-detox products report that the colour comes from the product reacting, with no body-derived waste found.[1]
